snippet.description:

During the Middle Ages, torture became an officially sanctioned tool of interrogation, used not just for punishment but for prying confessions from the accused. Its formal approval came in 1252, when the unsuitably named Pope Innocent IV authorised its use within the Church’s judicial procedures. 

From that moment, torture shifted from a shadowy practice to an institutionally endorsed method of extracting the ‘truth,’ shaping centuries of legal and religious investigations across Europe. Today we have delved into that brutal world to bring you a smattering of the worst torture methods from the Middle Ages.

snippet.title: How Peasants Survived Brutal Medieval Winters...
snippet.description:
Join from £3 on Patreon or YT Memberships for extra videos & bonus content, funded and influenced directly by you! https://www.patreon.com/cw/OfficialMedievalMadness

Surviving winter in the Middle Ages was brutal for those with little money. The medieval winter began after Martinmas on 11th of November and went on until Candlemas on the 2nd of February. That’s a long time to worry about food, heating and shelter, especially when there are no modern conveniences. Let’s travel back in time to the Middle Ages and take a look at how the poor tried to lessen the distress of a medieval winter with a lot of planning and a good deal of luck.

snippet.description:
Take a look at 3 English language grammar rules to find out where they come from and if you actually need to follow them.

--

Grammatical rules have caused heated debate in various regions and languages for centuries. But while we know people take grammar seriously, what’s less clear is, why? Where do these seemingly random rules come from, and which, if any, actually matter? Arika Okrent takes a closer look at three famous examples from the English language that have been the source of numerous grammatical arguments.

snippet.title: The Untold Truth of 1500s London: Beyond the Royals
snippet.description:
Step back in time and explore the bustling, vibrant streets of Tudor London. Discover what daily life in the 1500s was actually like, from the incredible boom in population to the birth of modern commercial theater.

If you love uncovering the hidden truths of history, make sure to hit that subscribe button so you never miss a journey into the past.

What this video covers:

The harsh reality of Tudor streets, unpaved roads, and daily survival.

How everyday Londoners worked, ate, and fought rampant diseases like the plague.

The wild entertainment scene, Shakespeare's Globe theater.

Earth-shattering events like the English Reformation.

Exploring the history of London reveals a rapidly expanding metropolis packed with over 200,000 people by the end of the century. We dive deep into sixteenth-century England to uncover the rigid social classes, the unique Tudor hobbies, and the incredible resilience of the people who built the foundation of the modern world. Whether you are fascinated by the medieval era or the explosive Tudor dynasty, this deep dive shows a side of the city you’ve never seen.

snippet.title: 9 Days in Hell: How 7,000 Elite Airborne Soldiers Were Abandoned
snippet.description:
In the late summer of 1944, Allied victory against Nazi Germany seemed absolute. The German Wehrmacht was retreating in chaos, Paris was free, and General Montgomery conceived a daring gamble to end World War II by Christmas. Codenamed Operation Market Garden, it was designed to be the largest airborne assault in human history, dropping 35,000 elite troops deep behind enemy lines to capture vital bridges and open a back door into the German heartland.

But a catastrophic failure in intelligence processing sent the British 1st Airborne Division dropping directly into a hornets' nest. Instead of facing weak reservists, the paratroopers landed on top of two highly disciplined SS Panzer divisions. Lieutenant Colonel John Frost and a mere 800 men managed to seize the northern end of the critical Arnhem bridge, but without immediate reinforcements or reliable supply drops, they were quickly surrounded by heavy armor and merciless artillery.

snippet.title: What causes avalanches, and can you survive them? - Simon Trautman
snippet.description:
Explore the three conditions needed to trigger an avalanche, and what makes these natural disasters so hard to survive.

--

Avalanches are the rapid descent of snow, ice, rock, or a combination of these down a slope. They can be destructive natural disasters and personal tragedies: killing an average of 27 people annually in the US. These alpine nightmares don’t just awaken out of nowhere; they need three specific conditions. So, what causes an avalanche? And is there any way to survive? Simon Trautman investigates.

Lesson by Simon Trautman, directed by Denys Spolitak.

snippet.title: The Brutal Reality of Medieval Surgery (Graphic Demo)
snippet.description:
What was it actually like to face the horrors of a medieval battlefield? Forget what you see in movies and video games. True historical combat was a nightmare of brutal trauma, high-impact arrow wounds, and agonizing infections. In this documentary, we look past the myth of the glamorous knight to explore the terrifying reality of medieval medical care.

Survival didn't just depend on the skill of your surgeon; it often depended on the size of your wallet. While wealthy lords brought elite master surgeons into the campaign, the common foot soldier had to rely on basic first aid or risk their life at the hands of rookies in the baggage train. From testing historical weapons on a realistic ballistic dummy to examining the actual tools used to saw bones and drill directly into human skulls, this episode reveals the agonizing choices injured soldiers had to face. Watch as we put ancient medical theories to the test—including a brutal Viking method for diagnosing fatal stomach wounds—and discover why avoiding the battlefield altogether was your absolute best chance at survival.

It has to be said, for the majority, life was damn cruel across the whole 1000 years of the time known to us as the Middle Ages. But conditions in medieval Europe didn’t just vary, they lurched from one extreme to another, depending on the century, the postcode, and whether you were born into lordship, land or labour. There were periods when life was pretty tolerable, with good harvests, fuller bellies and a faint glimmer of better living standards and opportunity. snippet.title: How Matera Became Italy's National Shame | Night Life of Matera's Stone Caves (AI Reconstruction)
snippet.description:
How 19th- and 20th-century poverty turned one of the world’s oldest cave settlements into Italy’s “national shame.” Follow the struggling farmers who lived with their animals in damp Sassi caves, battling drought, disease, and debt—until a shocking government relocation changed everything. A powerful story of endurance, forced change, and ultimate rebirth.

Lessons Learnt From This Video:
1) Economic neglect and unequal land systems can trap hardworking communities in centuries-old poverty even inside a modern nation.
2) Well-meaning relocation plans can destroy the very social bonds and rhythms that helped people survive the hardest times.
3) True progress demands more than new houses—it requires dignity, community, and respect for the people who endured the old ways.

Sources:
1) Smithsonian Magazine – “How Matera Went From Ancient Civilization to Slum to a Hidden Gem” (detailed conditions, relocation of ~16,000 people, De Gasperi’s 1950 visit).
2) Cortona International – “Matera – a history of poverty” (latifundia system, post-unification neglect, Carlo Levi’s impact).
3) Carlo Levi’s book Christ Stopped at Eboli (1945) – primary eyewitness account of cave living conditions and southern poverty that shocked Italy.
4) The Guardian – “The miracle of Matera” (2017) (personal stories, infant mortality, and post-1950s revival).

snippet.title: Were the Ottomans a Roman dynasty?
snippet.description:
The Ottomans considered themselves a continuation of the Roman empire. In this video I discuss how they could be understood in that way.

This video was sparked by a comment thread under https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NVkVG5CL-Go

My argument here is based on how the late Byzantines conceived of what it means to be Roman (Romans are people of Greek culture and religion, and the region where they live is the Land of the Romans). But there is one aspect of the Byzantine definition of "Roman" that I left out because it wasn't relevant to the Ottoman self-definition: the Byzantines believed that the Roman empire was first and foremost a Christian empire, and in fact the center and bulwark of the Christian faith in the world. Obviously the Ottomans did not see themselves in that light. In other words, the Byzantines and Ottomans disagreed on whether being Christian is a necessary part of being Roman.

===================================

FREQUENT OBJECTIONS IN THE COMMENTS

There are a couple remarks that keep showing up in the comments over and over again. Here are my responses.

*COMMENT: "Rumi wasn't from Anatolia! He was from Central Asia/Afghanistan!"*

In the English language, saying that someone is from a place doesn't always mean they were born there. It can mean a place where they currently live or where they have relocated to. For example, Barack Obama was 24 when he moved to Chicago, but we still say he is from Chicago. Rumi left Balkh at a young age (18 or 20 years old), and then lived in Anatolia for 50 years. According to the rules of English usage, it is correct to say he is from Anatolia.

And honestly, why do you think he's called Rumi, anyway? Maybe you should take a time machine back to the 13th century and tell everyone there to stop calling him Rumi, too. What the heck?

(By the way, if you want to hear about what Rumi's family was escaping from when they left Balkh, check out this video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gGDKO5xuJow.)

*COMMENT: "The France analogy is stupid! The French did the French Revolution to themselves! The Ottomans were outsiders who conquered!"*

I have three thoughts on this:

(1) If you listen to what I say in the video, you'll realize that this is irrelevant to my point. In the video I make the analogy in response to the objection that the Ottomans changed the "political ideology, political legitimacy, the legal system." For example, the Ottomans did not adopt the Roman legal code or carry on Byzantine court ceremonial. The basis of their legitimacy was different because unlike the Byzantine emperors, they were not self-proclaimed defenders of Christianity. Likewise, the basis for the French Republic's legitimacy was different, it changed France's laws and legal system, and it was no longer the defender of Catholicism.

I was not saying, and do not now claim, that the Ottoman takeover was like the French Revolution in every respect.

(2) Also, many commenters worded their objection in a way that betrayed some basic misunderstandings of the Byzantines and Ottomans themselves.
(2a) *"The Ottomans were foreigners! They came from Central Asia!"* The Turks had been in Anatolia for 400 years at that point, the same amount of time that white people have been in North America.
(2b) *"The Ottomans weren't ethnically Greek/Roman!"* That would not have mattered to the Byzantines. If the Turks had been Orthodox Christian instead of Muslim, then they would likely be regarded as one more in a long line of Byzantine dynastic usurpers and the 1453 takeover would not be famous today. The Byzantines didn't care about your genetics. They cared about whether you were Orthodox Christian. That said, by the 15th century the Turks and Greeks in Anatolia had mixed genetically. What made someone a "Turk" or "Greek" by that point wasn't their genetics but their lifestyle and family allegiances.

(3) *"The French Revolution was an internal development!"* This comment betrays a nationalist's logic. You're categorizing how severe the change is based on whether the people doing it are members or non-members of a given national group. *That is not how premodern people thought.* That is modern thinking which assumes that people naturally sort into "nationalities" and that their "nationalities" (whatever that means) are the ultimate basis for political legitimacy. Under this thinking, a "Turk" (defined nationalistically) can never be a Roman emperor because he belongs to the wrong nationality. That is how people today think, but that is not how people in the 15th century thought.

To give just one example of what I mean: In 1714 the British imported a German *who was not fluent in English* to be their king. Why? Because he wasn't Catholic. For the British, it was more important that their king be Protestant than that he be "ethnically" British. In other words, a Catholic Scotsman was for them more of an outsider than a Protestant German.

snippet.title: Mary Beard On The Insane Origins Of The Roman Empire
snippet.description:
The story of the Roman Empire is often told through grand marble columns and sweeping military conquests, but the true reality on the ground was far more complex, improvised, and brutal than the legends suggest. Long before the Colosseum was built, the early Romans laid the foundations of a global superpower using unique strategies of assimilation, massive infrastructure projects, and an aggressive military machine.

00:00 - Episode 1
From the bloody myths of Romulus and Remus to the rise of historic titans, Mary explores how Rome transformed the western world. Discover how a culture hardwired for conquest took down rival superpowers like Carthage, and how the weight of its own territory fractured its democracy, paving the way for Julius Caesar, a chaotic civil war, and the birth of Rome's first emperor, Augustus.

58:00 - Episode 2
This is the story of ancient globalization; from an 80,000 km network of superhighways and mind-boggling aqueducts to a massive single-currency oil economy. But beneath the glittering surface of wealth and luxury in cities like Ephesus lies a dark, uncomfortable truth.

snippet.title: How England Built The First Steam Engine and Changed the Whole World (AI Reconstruction)
snippet.description:
England didn't invent the steam engine because they were visionaries — they invented it because they were desperate. From a flooded coal mine in 1712 to locomotives tearing across the countryside, this is the real story of how one iron machine ended an entire way of human life and built the modern world from its ashes. The men who built it, the workers who suffered under it, and the world that was never the same again.

LESSONS LEARNED:
1) Necessity, not genius, is usually the true mother of invention
2) One small efficiency improvement (Watt's condenser) can reshape an entire civilization
3) Power without accountability always costs the powerless the most
4) Geography no longer limits human ambition once energy becomes portable
5) History rarely announces itself — it usually just sounds like a distant thud from a mine shaft

SOURCES:
Encyclopædia Britannica — Steam Engine (Newcomen's 1712 engine, Watt's condenser improvement, rotary motion development)
Science Museum Group (London) — History of the Steam Engine (Engine count by 1800, Luddite timeline 1811–1816)
Wellcome Collection, London — Public Health in Industrial England (Cholera outbreaks, living conditions in factory towns, child labor records)

snippet.title: Let's Talk About Cannibalism In The Middle Ages...
snippet.description:
Support our non AI content from £3 on Patreon or YT Memberships for extra videos & bonus content, funded and influenced directly by you! https://www.patreon.com/cw/OfficialMedievalMadness

For many people, when they think about medieval history, it conjures up thoughts of castles, jousts and chivalrous knights; the sort of stories told in historical dramas. The reality was a much more brutal world of war, siege, disease and famine, things that were a regular occurrence in the Middle Ages. During those times, something a lot darker was also happening, something hardly ever spoken about, one of the great social taboos. Cannibalism – the eating of human flesh. Cannibalism is often seen as a barbaric act, one of the most horrifying and cruel things that one human can do to another. 

One that was a million miles away from the gallant knights of the Middle Ages. However, medieval sources show that cannibalism wasn’t just an act carried out by starving peasants during times of famine. It was quite acceptable for parts of the human body to be used for medicinal purposes and as we shall see, cannibalism was also carried out just for the hell of it. Let’s travel back in time to the Middle Ages and take a look at what drove the Medievals to such extremes and what else they ate to stay alive. Welcome to Medieval Madness.

Narrated by James Wade
Written by Lisa E Rawcliffe 
Edited by Jamit Productions
Thank you for watching!

snippet.title: Dan Snow: How Hitler Defeated the World's Strongest Armies in 6 Weeks
snippet.description:
On May 10, 1940, Hitler unleashed the largest concentration of motorized vehicles in history, launching a devastating blitzkrieg that shattered Western Europe. In just six weeks, the mighty imperial powers of Britain and France were brought to their knees. How did the Allied forces, despite having more tanks, guns, and men, collapse so rapidly? In this deep-dive military documentary, we break down "Case Yellow" (Fall Gelb)—the audacious and risky German gamble through the "impenetrable" Ardennes forest that bypassed the Maginot Line, trapped the Allies at Dunkirk, and forced a humiliating French surrender in the historic railway carriage at Compiègne. Discover how outmoded tactics, shattered communications, and sheer psychological terror redefined the face of modern warfare forever, leaving Great Britain to stand entirely alone against the Nazi war machine.

snippet.description:
I use the example of the wheelbarrow to talk about some general points about the history of technology, and the limits to our ability to reasonably make sweeping generalizations about individual technologies.

0:00 Some people overestimate how necessary wheelbarrows are
3:53 Technologies are only obvious in hindsight
7:23 It's really hard to trace the origins of a technology
